claims.text: Adding approximately 0.5–1 at.% Y2O3 nanoparticles to a refractory high-entropy alloy will improve its high-temperature mechanical capability.
The Y2O3 addition will minimally affect alloy density.
The Y2O3 addition will preserve room-temperature mechanical performance.
Processing will produce stable nanoscale Y2O3 dispersoids distributed uniformly within the metallic matrix.
Y2O3 dispersoids will hinder dislocation motion through pinning.
Y2O3 dispersoids will impede grain-boundary sliding at elevated temperatures.
Dislocation and grain-boundary pinning will increase high-temperature strength.
The intervention will improve creep resistance under sustained loading at approximately 900–1100°C.
The intervention will increase high-temperature yield strength relative to the untreated alloy.
High-temperature mechanical properties are expected to improve by approximately 10–20% relative to the untreated alloy.
A refractory high-entropy alloy without oxide dispersion strengthening has lower creep resistance than the proposed Y2O3-containing alloy.
A refractory high-entropy alloy without oxide dispersion strengthening has lower high-temperature mechanical stability than the proposed Y2O3-containing alloy.
Y2O3 concentrations above the proposed range could cause embrittlement.
Y2O3 concentrations above the proposed range could cause significant density increases.
The beneficial effects are confined to an approximately 0.5–1 at.% Y2O3 compositional window.
The magnitude of improvement and optimal Y2O3 content may depend on alloy composition and processing conditions.
The proposed test compares an untreated control with a 0.5–1 at.% Y2O3-containing material at 1000°C under identical stress conditions.

contradictions.description: The loading is described as a small volume fraction but quantified in at.%; volume fraction and atomic percent are distinct concentration measures, so the specified intervention is internally ambiguous.
